frictionVectors.title: European Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains a critical market for Algerian gas, creating leverage but also exposure to pricing pressure and long-term shifts toward liquefied natural gas and renewables.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Energy Technology
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong state control over hydrocarbons, while relying on foreign partners for investment, enhanced recovery, and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Revenue Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Angola remains highly dependent on offshore oil revenues, leaving public finances and sovereign policy vulnerable to production declines and global price volatility.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure and financing continue to support connectivity, but debt servicing and project dependence constrain fiscal and strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Transit Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger and wider Sahel instability threaten transit flows through the Port of Cotonou, exposing Benin's trade model to political decisions beyond its borders.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Capital
frictionVectors.details: Port, logistics, and energy expansion depend substantially on foreign investors and lenders, limiting domestic control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond Market Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana exercises unusually strong state influence over diamond revenues, but dependence on a concentrated global market leaves sovereignty exposed to demand shocks and pricing power.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Prospective copper, nickel, and other mineral projects could diversify exports, while attracting foreign capital that may challenge local value-addition goals.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgent Threat to Mining
frictionVectors.details: Armed-group activity and insecurity disrupt mining zones, transport corridors, and state revenue collection, weakening practical control over gold resources.

frictionVectors.title: Rebalancing Foreign Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater national control over mining while reducing reliance on Western partners and deepening security ties with Russia, creating new dependency risks.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Critical Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking foreign capital for nickel, rare-earth, and gold projects, but limited state capacity and opaque contracts could leave it with weak control over value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Security Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain tense, while instability in eastern DRC creates security and trade risks that constrain Burundi's economic sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, European, and other external partners compete for influence around ports, logistics, and maritime-security infrastructure, giving Praia leverage but also creating dependency risks.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Food Import Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's island geography leaves it dependent on imported fuel and food; renewable expansion improves resilience but has not removed exposure to external prices and financing.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Resource Chains
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, timber, and emerging mining projects rely heavily on foreign firms and external finance, limiting domestic capture of value despite Cameroon's formal ownership of resources.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict and Infrastructure Risk
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts roads, agriculture, and investment while complicating state control over resource corridors and border trade.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security-for-Resources Model
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security structures provide regime protection while expanding influence around gold and diamond networks, reducing transparency and limiting independent state control.

frictionVectors.title: Artisanal Mining and Regional Smuggling
frictionVectors.details: Weak enforcement allows minerals to move through neighboring states and informal networks, while insecurity keeps much of the country's resource base outside effective government administration.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Dependence and Foreign Operators
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal system remains highly dependent on oil produced and marketed through foreign-linked infrastructure, leaving national budgets exposed to contract terms and price shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Spillover and Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan war strains eastern border security and humanitarian capacity, while shifting ties with France, Russia, and other partners create competing external pressures over military access and strategic infrastructure.

highlights: External financing sustains limited state capacity

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and maritime sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, while Comoros continues to contest its sovereignty and faces migration and maritime-security tensions around the island.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country relies heavily on remittances, Gulf and multilateral assistance, and foreign-funded infrastructure, limiting autonomous control over strategic development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and copper leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and trading networks dominate much of the value chain for copper and cobalt, while Kinshasa is seeking greater local processing, contract leverage, and fiscal control.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern armed-group and regional pressure
frictionVectors.details: M23-related conflict, allegations of external backing, and weak state access to the east continue to undermine territorial sovereignty and disrupt mining and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: State finances and political stability remain heavily tied to oil production, leaving national resource control vulnerable to price cycles, foreign operators, and opaque revenue management.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-finance exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese participation in roads, ports, and public works expands connectivity but can increase debt, procurement, and strategic dependence on external contractors and lenders.

highlights: Cocoa and mining value capture is improving

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire is strengthening processing and farmer-income policies, but global traders and processors still retain substantial influence over pricing and downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital and strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rapid port, energy, and transport expansion depends on multinational investment and lenders, creating exposure to external commercial priorities despite stronger domestic institutions.

highlights: Ports remain vital but externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military footprint
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, France, Japan, and other partners use Djibouti-based facilities, giving the government revenue and leverage while constraining strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt concentration
frictionVectors.details: The economy depends heavily on logistics, leases, and externally financed port infrastructure, with Chinese-linked assets and debt creating persistent sovereignty and restructuring risks.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service obligations and IMF-linked reforms give Gulf states, multilateral lenders, and strategic investors greater leverage over economic policy and state assets.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile Allocation
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam remains a core sovereignty and water-security concern, despite continued diplomatic engagement.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Decline
frictionVectors.details: Falling legacy oil output and limited new investment are reducing fiscal autonomy while foreign operators retain influence over remaining offshore production.

frictionVectors.title: China-Linked Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Major infrastructure and construction ties with Chinese firms provide strategic assets but may increase financing, maintenance, and concession-related dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Port and Border Rivalries
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's Red Sea position exposes it to competition involving Ethiopia, Sudan, Gulf actors, and other external powers over ports, access, and military influence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide hard currency but concentrate resource-sector capacity and revenue channels in partnerships with foreign mining companies.

frictionVectors.title: SACU and South Africa Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Customs receipts, electricity links, logistics, and market access remain heavily tied to South Africa, limiting independent policy space and resilience.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Water Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial growth is constrained by dependence on imported power and regional water systems, creating exposure to South African supply conditions and infrastructure bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Debt Restructuring and External Finance
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressures and restructuring negotiations with international creditors constrain fiscal sovereignty while opening space for external influence over economic reforms.

frictionVectors.title: Port Access and Regional Security
frictionVectors.details: Landlocked Ethiopia's search for reliable Red Sea access intensifies tensions with neighbors, particularly Somalia and Eritrea, and attracts competing Gulf and other foreign interests.

highlights: Railway and Port Sovereignty Under Pressure

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The post-junta government is seeking greater state participation and local processing in manganese, iron ore, and oil. This risks friction with established French, Chinese, and other foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Trans-Gabon Railway Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The railway remains essential for moving manganese and other commodities to export terminals, leaving the state vulnerable to foreign financing, concession terms, and infrastructure bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Banjul Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: The port is strategically important but constrained by capacity and logistics, encouraging reliance on external investors and neighboring Senegalese corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew and Groundnut Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Foreign buyers and limited domestic processing capture much of the value from agricultural exports. The government has limited fiscal space to enforce stronger local-content rules.

highlights: Cocoa and Oil Sovereignty Under Strain

frictionVectors.title: Galamsey and Mining Governance
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining is damaging water systems and agricultural land while exposing gaps in state enforcement. Foreign-linked equipment, informal financiers, and domestic political networks complicate efforts to regain control.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and External Financing Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms limit policy flexibility over energy, mining, and public infrastructure. Recovery depends heavily on commodity prices and continued external confidence.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Infrastructure Bargain
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project is bringing railways, ports, and major foreign capital, but the scale of Chinese and multinational participation raises concerns over revenue capture, debt exposure, and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Contract Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Guinea is pressing operators for local refining, infrastructure delivery, and stricter compliance while remaining dependent on foreign firms for technology, financing, and export logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Export Capture
frictionVectors.details: The economy depends heavily on raw cashew exports, with foreign traders and processors capturing much of the value. Weak regulation and limited storage and processing capacity restrict sovereign bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Political Instability and Port Access
frictionVectors.details: Institutional volatility undermines long-term infrastructure planning and invites external influence through security assistance, port projects, and commercial concessions.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and Chinese, Gulf, and Western infrastructure finance constrain Nairobi's policy room. Debt-service pressures continue to influence port, rail, and energy decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu Corridor Security
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu Port-South Sudan-Ethiopia corridor remains strategically valuable but exposed to al-Shabaab attacks, regional instability, and competing external commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water-export relationship with South Africa provides vital revenue but gives Pretoria substantial leverage over infrastructure, pricing, and security cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Border Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains exposed to external apparel markets and South African logistics, leaving jobs and customs revenue vulnerable to trade-policy shifts.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Concession Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining agreements, especially in iron ore, generate export revenue but leave Liberia dependent on foreign operators, concession terms, and commodity cycles.

frictionVectors.title: Monrovia Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Control of port services and transport links remains sensitive as Liberia seeks investment while protecting customs authority and local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Oil Authorities
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation and rival security structures continue to threaten unified control of the National Oil Corporation, export terminals, and revenue distribution.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Entrenchment
frictionVectors.details: Turkish, Russian, and other external security relationships shape access to bases, energy assets, and transport corridors, limiting Libya's independent strategic choices.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and Cobalt Dependency
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led mining projects provide export earnings and infrastructure but leave Madagascar exposed to external ownership, commodity volatility, and limited domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Illicit Timber and Coastal Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Illegal rosewood networks, offshore resource interests, and weak enforcement continue to erode state control over high-value environmental assets.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on IMF and donor support limit Malawi's room to set independent fiscal and development priorities. Currency pressure and import shortages amplify exposure to external conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Sovereignty Gap
frictionVectors.details: Interest in uranium, rare earths, and other minerals is rising, but weak processing capacity and infrastructure could leave Malawi dependent on foreign capital and exporting low-value ores.

highlights: Gold sector remains vulnerable to capture

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Bamako's reliance on Russian-linked security support has reduced Western leverage but increases dependence on an external military partner. Persistent jihadist violence continues to weaken state control over transport and mining zones.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Revenue and Informal Mining
frictionVectors.details: Gold is central to Mali's fiscal survival, yet informal production, opaque contracting, and security-linked extraction limit transparent public capture of resource rents. Disputes with foreign mining operators remain a major sovereignty fault line.

highlights: Gas production opens a new strategic window

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Partnership
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project can strengthen Mauritania's fiscal position, but offshore gas development leaves the country reliant on foreign operators, export infrastructure, and stable relations with Senegal.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Logistics Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and prospective green-hydrogen projects require large foreign-backed transport, port, and energy investments. Weak domestic processing risks preserving an enclave model with limited local value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Sovereignty and Security
frictionVectors.details: The Chagos issue remains tied to Mauritius's territorial claims, the future of Diego Garcia, and wider Indian Ocean security calculations. Any settlement must balance sovereign rights with the strategic interests of external powers.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance and Blue Economy
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius benefits from diversified services, investment, and maritime links, but its small market and dependence on external capital leave it exposed to shifts in global finance, tourism, and ocean-resource governance.

highlights: Phosphate and energy chains remain strategic assets

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control and development of Western Sahara underpin major port, renewable-energy, and mineral strategies, but remain contested by the Polisario Front and subject to international legal and diplomatic scrutiny.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, European, Gulf, and other external investors support ports, rail, energy, and manufacturing. This strengthens Morocco's capabilities while creating exposure to competing foreign interests and supply-chain leverage.

highlights: Cabo Delgado insurgency constrains LNG recovery
Resource nationalism rises around gas and mining

frictionVectors.title: LNG Security and Foreign Contractors
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence and offshore gas-security requirements keep Mozambique dependent on foreign energy firms, contractors, and external military assistance. Delayed LNG exports limit state leverage over future gas revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Corridor Governance
frictionVectors.details: Coal, graphite, and rubies attract international capital while weak local processing and transport infrastructure constrain domestic value capture. Community grievances remain concentrated around land access and revenue distribution.

highlights: Critical minerals draw competing strategic investors
Green hydrogen ambitions test state capacity

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Critical-Mineral Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign ownership remains central to uranium, lithium, and emerging rare-earth projects, creating exposure to global commodity cycles and external processing capacity. Windhoek is seeking stronger local beneficiation without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Large projects rely on European, Gulf, and other external finance, technology, and offtake agreements. Port, water, and transmission constraints could leave Namibia supplying low-value inputs rather than controlling the full energy chain.

highlights: Junta tightens control over uranium and extractives

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are pressing foreign operators for greater state control and fiscal returns, particularly in uranium, while political ties with Western partners have deteriorated. Regulatory uncertainty and security risks threaten production and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Export Corridors Under Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The loss of dependable regional partnerships and continuing militant threats complicate oil and mineral export routes. Niger remains exposed to border closures, sanctions risk, and dependence on neighboring states' ports and pipelines.

highlights: Oil-sector reform improves state leverage unevenly
Power and pipeline insecurity erode resource sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria needs international capital and technology to sustain deepwater production and develop gas, limiting its bargaining power despite regulatory reforms. Contract disputes, local-content demands, and revenue pressures remain persistent.

frictionVectors.title: Grid, Pipeline, and Refining Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity, pipeline vandalism, and theft continue to reduce the value captured from domestic energy resources. New refining capacity improves resilience, but fuel logistics and transmission infrastructure remain vulnerable.

highlights: Regional security role expands Kigali's leverage

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security influence in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo remains tied to accusations that it facilitates access to conflict-linked minerals, generating sustained diplomatic and sanctions pressure. Kigali denies systematic exploitation and frames its posture around border security.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Dependence on External Finance
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure, technology, and mineral-processing initiatives rely heavily on foreign donors, investors, and Gulf and Western partnerships. This supports rapid development but leaves fiscal and strategic space vulnerable to political conditionality.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore exploration dependence
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe remains reliant on foreign operators and licensing partners to assess potentially valuable offshore blocks. Commercial discoveries have not yet translated into meaningful sovereign revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic maritime competition
frictionVectors.details: External actors are seeking influence through maritime security, fisheries, port access, and development assistance. The country has limited institutional capacity to balance competing partners while protecting its maritime domain.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production has strengthened Dakar's leverage, but disputes over contract terms, local content, and revenue transparency could unsettle relations with international operators and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure financing
frictionVectors.details: Large transport, energy, and port projects rely on foreign capital and contractors, including Gulf, European, Chinese, and multilateral partners. Debt sustainability and strategic control of logistics assets remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of fisheries value chains
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles retains formal control over its waters, but foreign fleets, processing interests, and vessel-financing arrangements shape the returns from tuna and other marine resources. Enforcement capacity remains a constraint.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean security partnerships
frictionVectors.details: The country balances security and infrastructure relationships involving India, the United States, China, France, and Gulf actors. Port access, surveillance systems, and maritime cooperation can generate domestic concern over strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Large-scale mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, bauxite, and related projects remain central to export earnings and are dominated by foreign capital and technical operators. Fiscal gains are vulnerable to commodity cycles, tax disputes, and weak domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-resources exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mining corridors, roads, ports, and power investments increasingly tie national development to external investors and lenders. The government faces pressure to secure jobs and infrastructure while preventing enclaves and opaque concessions.

highlights: Port diplomacy collides with security threats

frictionVectors.title: Ethiopia-Somaliland maritime dispute
frictionVectors.details: Mogadishu continues to reject arrangements granting Ethiopia maritime access through Somaliland, viewing them as a breach of Somali territorial sovereignty. The dispute risks drawing in Turkey, the Gulf states, and other regional security actors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign security and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and other partners provide military, maritime, or infrastructure support, but their rival interests complicate unified national control. Al-Shabaab attacks and limited state capacity continue to constrain the commercial and strategic value of ports.

frictionVectors.title: POWER AND GRID BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and delayed grid expansion constrain mining, manufacturing, and data infrastructure. Private and foreign investment is increasingly shaping energy recovery, limiting Pretoria's room to dictate terms.

frictionVectors.title: PORTS, RAIL, AND MINERAL ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Transnet's rail and port weaknesses reduce sovereign control over mineral exports and strengthen the bargaining position of multinational logistics and mining firms. Competition among China, the United States, Europe, and Gulf investors is intensifying around strategic minerals.

highlights: Peace process tied to pipeline security

frictionVectors.title: OIL PIPELINE VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's export lifeline runs through conflict-affected Sudan, exposing national revenue to disruptions and decisions made by external transit authorities. Chinese and other foreign oil operators retain major leverage over production and technical infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: ELITE CONTROL OF RESOURCE REVENUES
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation, delayed elections, and armed competition make oil revenues vulnerable to opaque allocation and diversion. Limited domestic refining and transport capacity deepen dependence on foreign firms and neighboring states.

highlights: War fragments gold and port sovereignty
Red Sea access drives external rivalry

frictionVectors.title: GOLD WAR ECONOMY
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling finance rival armed networks while creating channels for external commercial and political influence. Gulf-linked trading routes and foreign buyers can capture value that bypasses formal state institutions.

frictionVectors.title: PORT SUDAN AND RED SEA COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan and associated corridors is strategically important to the warring parties and to outside powers seeking Red Sea access. Foreign military, logistical, and diplomatic support risks converting infrastructure decisions into instruments of the conflict.

highlights: LNG and corridors remain strategic tests

frictionVectors.title: LNG TERMS AND SOVEREIGN CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations over large offshore gas development continue to balance fiscal returns, local-content demands, and investor certainty. The scale of foreign capital and technology required could constrain Tanzania's ability to maximize domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND TRANSPORT CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Dar es Salaam-linked rail and port projects are drawing competing Chinese, Gulf, European, and regional interests. Tanzania gains leverage from diversification, but debt, concession, and access terms remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional logistics hub

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCE AND FOREIGN CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé gives Togo outsized regional influence but also makes customs, logistics, and terminal operations sensitive to foreign concessionaires and external trade flows. Competition among Turkish, Chinese, European, and Gulf-linked actors is likely to shape expansion decisions.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE AND SAHEL SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Togo's phosphate sector provides strategic revenue but has limited downstream processing and remains exposed to external markets. Spillover from militant activity in northern Togo and neighboring Burkina Faso raises costs for transport and resource infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: EU financial and migration pressure
frictionVectors.details: European funding and market access remain linked to Tunisia's cooperation on irregular migration, narrowing Tunis's room for independent economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on imported gas and electricity, alongside slow renewable deployment, limits Tunisia's control over energy security and exposes it to external price shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Tilenga and EACOP dependency
frictionVectors.details: Uganda's oil strategy depends heavily on TotalEnergies, CNOOC, and the Tanzania export corridor, creating financing, environmental, and sovereignty pressures around first production.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure financing
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy projects expand connectivity but can increase repayment exposure and foreign influence over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is attracting competing investment from Chinese, Gulf, Western, and regional actors in copper and battery minerals, raising pressure over ownership, taxation, and local processing.

frictionVectors.title: Power supply vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortages and climate-related volatility constrain mining output and increase dependence on regional electricity imports and emergency infrastructure finance.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of strategic minerals
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain prominent in lithium, platinum, and other mining ventures, while Zimbabwe struggles to secure transparent contracts, reliable taxation, and meaningful domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and sanctions exposure
frictionVectors.details: Currency instability, restricted access to global finance, and sanctions-related risks raise dependence on politically aligned lenders and opaque mineral-backed arrangements.
